q: You are steering with a tiller and want the bow to turn to port. Which way do you move the tiller?
a: To starboard
o: To port
Straight back towards you
Hold it central and wait
why: A tiller works the opposite way: push it to starboard and the bow swings to port.

q: You are steering with a wheel and want to turn to starboard. Which way do you turn it?
a: Clockwise, like a car
o: Anticlockwise, the opposite way
Either way: the rudder finds the course
Anticlockwise, then back to the centre
why: A wheel steers like a car: turn it to starboard to go to starboard.

q: You call "Ready about" and the crew answer "Ready". What do you call as you put the helm over?
a: "Lee-oh!"
o: "Gybe-oh!"
"Ready about!" again
"Let go!"
why: "Lee-oh" (or "Helm's a-lee") tells the crew the bow is now turning through the wind.

q: The engine is off, there is no wind and the boat is drifting. You turn the wheel but the bow does not answer. Why?
a: No water is flowing past the rudder
o: The wheel needs turning much faster
The rudder only works under engine
The wheel has come off the rudder
why: A rudder steers only when water flows over it: no way on, no steering.

q: You have just taken the wheel. Which way do you turn?
a: To starboard, about 10°
o: To port, about 10°
To starboard, about 140°
Neither: the compass will catch up
why: Headings grow clockwise: to go from 130° to 140°, turn 10° to starboard.

q: The skipper gives you 090° towards a headland 8 miles away. The compass swings in the waves and is tiring to watch. What helps?
a: Steer for a landmark on 090° and check the compass now and then
o: Chase every swing of the compass card
Steer by the wake astern and ignore the compass
Steer for the nearest boat on that side
why: A fixed landmark is steadier to steer for; the compass confirms you are still on course.

q: You are steering and see this on the genoa. What do you do with the helm?
a: Bear away a little until both stream
o: Luff up a little until both stream
Hold this heading: all is well
Tack at once onto the other tack
why: A lifting windward tell-tale means you are too close to the wind: bear away.

q: The skipper asks you to sail as close to the wind as you can. How do you find the limit?
a: Head up slowly until the genoa luff lifts, then bear away a touch
o: Head up until the boat stops, then hold that heading
Bear away until the boat heels hard, then hold it
Steer straight into the wind and wait
why: The edge of the no-go zone is where the luff starts to lift; just below it the sails drive.

q: On a run, the skipper asks you to gybe. What do you call, and when?
a: "Ready to gybe", wait for "Ready", then "Gybe-oh" as you turn
o: "Gybe-oh", turn at once, then "Ready to gybe"
"Ready about", wait for "Ready", then "Lee-oh"
"Ready to gybe", then turn without waiting
why: Warn, wait for every crew member to answer, then call as the stern goes through the wind.

q: You are helming into a crowded marina under engine. What speed do you keep?
a: Slow, but enough to keep steering
o: Brisk, for good control in the wind
None: engine in neutral, drifting in
Whatever the skipper set out at sea
why: Go no faster than you would be happy to hit something at, but keep enough way to steer.

q: Motoring slowly astern, you want the stern to swing to starboard. Which way do you turn the wheel?
a: To starboard: astern, the stern follows the wheel
o: To port: astern, the steering is reversed
Amidships: going astern you cannot steer
To port, then give a burst ahead
why: Going astern with a wheel, turn it the way you want the stern to go.

q: You are at the wheel and put the engine into reverse. What do you expect first?
a: The stern swings to port before she gathers way
o: The stern swings to starboard at first
The bow swings to port at first
Nothing until you turn the wheel
why: Prop walk pushes the stern sideways in reverse, most of all before the boat is moving.

q: Two crew are working at the mast, sorting out a halyard. You are on the helm. What do you do?
a: Hold a steady course and warn them before any turn
o: Steer for the smoothest water, turning often
Speed up so they are finished sooner
Leave the helm for a moment to help them
why: Sudden turns or heel throw crew on deck off balance; keep her steady and call any change.

q: Under engine, the skipper asks you to hold the boat head to wind while the crew hoist the main. How do you know you are head to wind?
a: The masthead wind arrow points dead ahead
o: The boom swings out to one side
The genoa sheet goes tight
The wind is on the back of your neck
why: Head to wind, the wind comes over the bow, so the masthead arrow points straight forward.

q: On your first spell at the wheel, the boat wanders 20° either side of the course. What helps most?
a: Small, early corrections, then wait for her to answer
o: Big turns of the wheel to get back quickly
Holding the wheel rigid, never moving it
Steering by the compass only, never ahead
why: A boat answers the helm slowly; small early corrections stop you over-steering.

q: You call "Ready about". One crew answers "Ready", but the one on the other sheet is still putting turns on the winch. What do you do?
a: Wait until everyone has answered "Ready"
o: Tack anyway: one crew member is enough
Call "Lee-oh" louder and start the turn
Tack, and let them catch up after
why: Only start the turn when every crew member has answered "Ready".

q: A wave pushes the stern on this course. Which turn of the bow risks an accidental gybe?
a: A turn to starboard, towards the boom
o: A turn to port, away from the boom
Any turn at all, either way
None: on a run the boom cannot cross
why: Turning towards the boom side takes the stern through the wind, and the boom slams across.

q: You are steering with a tiller from the windward side. The skipper says "Bear away a little". Which way do you move the tiller?
a: Towards you, to windward
o: Away from you, towards the boom
It depends which tack you are on
Hold it central: the sheets steer
why: Tiller to windward turns the bow to leeward, away from the wind: that is bearing away.

q: The skipper beside you asks what you would do. What is the best answer?
a: A short burst ahead, to push water over the rudder
o: Engine to neutral, and wait for the wind to drop
Turn the wheel hard over the other way
A long burst astern to stop the boat
why: Too slow, the rudder has no grip; a burst of propeller wash over it brings the steering back.

fig.title: Entering the marina
lines: The bow is blowing off sideways

q: Anna is taking over the helm from you. What do you tell her?
a: The course, the wind, and the ferry ahead
o: Only the course: she can see the rest
Only the ferry: the course can wait
How long you steered, and the boat speed
why: A handover gives the course, the wind and sail trim, and any traffic to watch.
